results.result: Centrosomes separate from the midplane in Xenopus eggs and this movement is modeled in egg extracts. In eggs, centrosomes move hundreds of microns over tens of minutes at ~10 µm/min, while the interaction zone remains stationary. In extracts, MTOCs that are close together tend to move apart, modeling centrosome separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5, C21, C22, and C104 collectively establish that centrosome separation occurs in eggs and is successfully modeled in extracts. The data from fixed eggs (C1, Figure 1A-C), observations in extracts (C21, C22), and speed measurements (C104) provide converging evidence. The extract system is explicitly stated to model egg behavior based on hundreds of observations.

results.result: MTOC separation movement in egg extracts is driven by both dynein and actomyosin forces, with similar contributions from each. Inhibiting either motor system alone causes partial blockage, while inhibiting both causes almost complete blockage of movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by systematic inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2C. The quantitative analysis demonstrates that single inhibition of either dynein (p150-CC1) or F-actin (Cytochalasin D) partially blocks movement with similar effects on separation speed vs. distance slopes, while double inhibition causes near-complete blockage. The interpretation (C30) follows logically from the experimental data.

results.result: All cytoplasmic networks (MTs, ER, F-actin, and organelles) move together during aster separation in egg extracts. The networks move in the same direction at similar speeds of up to 7 µm/min, always directed away from the interaction zone on both sides of the aster.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 and C92 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including kymograph analysis (Figure 3C), PIV velocity measurements (Figure 3D), and visual inspection across >10 independent experiments. The co-movement is consistently observed across all three cytoplasmic networks and organelles visible in DIC, with velocities measured quantitatively by PIV showing similar speeds and directions.

results.result: The observed co-movement of cytoplasmic networks is inconsistent with the classic length-dependent pulling model, which predicts that organelles on the leading side should move toward the interaction zone or remain stationary, not move away from it.
results.evaluation: Claims C36 and C128 present a logical inference comparing observed data to model predictions. The data clearly show all networks moving away from the interaction zone (C35, Figure 3C,D), which directly contradicts the length-dependent pulling model's prediction that organelles should move inward or remain stationary. This is a valid interpretation of the discrepancy between observation and theory.

results.result: Asters do not move as completely rigid bodies but deform as gels, with spatial variation in velocity showing local compression and stretching. The region near interaction zones moves ~20% faster than the MTOC, while the leading edge moves ~20% slower.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 are supported by quantitative velocity analysis showing spatial variation within moving asters. The ~20% differences in velocity at different locations (C39) provide direct evidence for deformation rather than rigid body motion. The interpretation as gel-like behavior (C40) is reasonable given the observed velocity gradients.

results.result: At 60x magnification, some local ER segments exhibit rapid saltatory movement and transient deformation, but co-movement of cytoplasmic networks predominates even at this higher resolution. MT speckles, ER, and F-actin features slide outwards together in radial kymographs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by high-magnification imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Videos 1 and 4). The observations reconcile apparent contradictions with literature by showing that while local exceptions exist, the predominant behavior is co-movement even at higher spatiotemporal resolution. The citation to Ishihara et al., 2014 regarding dynein-driven outward sliding strengthens C43.

results.result: On HOOK2-functionalized coverslips, dynein generates pulling forces that cause asters to exhibit rapid circular oscillatory movement at ~1 µm/s. All cytoskeletal networks (MTs, ER, F-actin, keratin) move together with the moving asters, demonstrating mechanical integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 describe a complementary experimental system supported by extensive data (Figure 4, Videos 5-6). The circular movement is reproducible (>10 experiments), blocked by dynein inhibition (C47), and shows complete co-movement of all networks by kymograph and PIV analysis (C48, Figure 4E,F). The conclusion of mechanical integration (C50) is well-supported by the consistent co-movement across multiple cytoplasmic components.

results.result: IP-MS experiments show that anti-HOOK2 pulls down HOOK2, HOOK3, and multiple dynein-dynactin complex subunits in interphase extracts. The interaction between HOOK2 and dynein-dynactin is greatly reduced in mitotic extracts, suggesting negative regulation by CDK1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by quantitative IP-MS data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) from multiple biological replicates (3 interphase, 2 mitotic, 3 IgG controls). The identification of HOOK2 as most abundant, HOOK3 detection consistent with heterodimerization, and cell cycle-dependent changes in dynein-dynactin binding are all directly shown in the data. The inference about CDK1 regulation (C54) is reasonable given the mitotic vs. interphase comparison.

results.result: Photo-released fluorescein disperses within tens of seconds by diffusion, validating it as a freely diffusing small molecule probe. The center of the fluorescein cloud tracks with the moving MTOC, demonstrating that cytosol advects with moving asters. Cytosol viscosity is estimated at ~6x that of water.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by the caged fluorescein experiments (Figure 5, Video 7). The diffusion analysis (C55, C56, Figure 5D,E) validates the probe behavior and enables viscosity estimation (C57) consistent with literature. The tracking of cloud center with MTOC (C58, Figure 5F) across >10 experiments in 3 extracts provides strong evidence for cytosol advection (C59). Statistical analysis mentioned in methods addresses potential tracking errors.

results.result: Inward flow along the interaction zone was observed around separating asters, consistent with hydrodynamic forces from moving asters. Advection of cytosol suggests a poroelastic regime with an effective pore size upper bound of ~100 nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C60 and C61 are supported by PIV analysis of DIC images (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and theoretical calculations in the methods. The observed inward flow (C60) is consistent with the expected compensatory flows from aster movement. The poroelastic analysis (C61) uses appropriate physical parameters (velocity, viscosity, elastic modulus) to estimate pore size, with calculations detailed in methods.

results.result: In control extracts with intact F-actin, most organelles (ER, mitochondria, acidic organelles) remain evenly distributed over growing asters. A small fraction of ER accumulates near MTOCs (~2-fold enrichment). Astral MTs induce subtle changes in ER texture and cause transient radial alignment of F-actin bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by imaging data from control conditions (Figures 6A, 7A,D, Videos 8-9). The quantitative measurement of ~2-fold ER enrichment (C64, Figure 6A') is based on >5 examples. The subtle textural changes in ER (C65) and F-actin alignment (C66) are documented in videos and consistent with previous work (Field et al., 2019 for C66).

results.result: When F-actin is fragmented with Cytochalasin D, all organelles exhibit inward movement that is fastest at the growing aster periphery. Compared to control, a greater fraction of ER is transported inward at speeds an order of magnitude faster, accumulating to ~6-fold enrichment near MTOCs with ~30% depletion at the periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 are strongly supported by systematic comparison between control and Cytochalasin D conditions (Figures 6B, 7G, Videos 10-11). The quantitative measurements of ER enrichment (~6-fold, C71), peripheral depletion (~30%, C72), and order of magnitude speed increase (C70) are directly shown in the data. The observation that movement is fastest at the periphery (C68) is supported by multiple analysis methods (Figure 7).

results.result: The ER and potentially all organelles recruit dynein and can move toward MTOCs, but this inward movement is restrained by F-actin under control conditions. With dynein inhibition (p150-CC1), organelles move neither inwards nor outwards, indicating dynein generates the majority of force on organelles.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are supported by the combination of Cytochalasin D and p150-CC1 experiments (Figures 6, 7). The dramatic increase in organelle movement when F-actin is fragmented (C67-C73) supports the restraining role of F-actin (C76). The complete block of movement with p150-CC1 (C78, Figure 6C) strongly supports dynein as the major force generator (C79). The observation that most organelles remain distributed even with F-actin fragmented (C77) is important for the overall interpretation.

results.result: Organelles exhibit a burst of inward movement when first contacted by the growing aster periphery, then slow or halt inside asters. Under control conditions, this burst was observed in 64% of extracts (7/11). With F-actin fragmented, the burst was observed in all experiments (>10 repeats), reaching velocities of ~0.25 µm/s and mass transport of 2% of total per min.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by multiple analysis methods (kymographs, PIV, mass transport) shown in Figure 7 and videos. The quantitative assessment across 11 extract preparations (C81) provides statistical context for the variability in control conditions. The consistent observation with F-actin fragmented (C82) and quantitative measurements of velocity and mass transport (C83, C84, Figure 7I,J) are well-documented.

results.result: Artificial dynein-coated beads (anti-HOOK2 beads) move inwards at constant speeds throughout asters: 0.2 ± 0.1 µm/s with F-actin intact and 0.7 ± 0.2 µm/s (threefold faster) with F-actin fragmented. Unlike organelles, these beads are transported all the way to the MTOC without slowing inside asters.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by quantitative tracking of artificial beads (Figure 8, Video 12). The constant speed measurements (C85, C86) with error estimates indicate proper statistical analysis. The comparison showing F-actin slows beads like organelles (C87) but beads don't slow inside asters like organelles do (C88) is a key observation that helps identify the role of F-actin vs. other braking mechanisms.

results.result: As organelles are transported toward MTOCs, fluorescent dextran is displaced away from MTOCs, consistent with volume conservation. However, the dextran signal is only reduced by ~10% and exclusion is only observed within ~50 µm of MTOCs, suggesting volume exclusion is unlikely to account for organelles becoming stationary inside asters.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are supported by dextran exclusion experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Video 13). The observation of dextran displacement (C89) is consistent with volume conservation. The quantitative measurements showing only ~10% reduction and ~50 µm exclusion zone (C90) support the conclusion that volume exclusion is not the primary mechanism for organelle halting (C91). This is a well-reasoned negative result that rules out a potential mechanism.

results.result: Co-movement of cytoplasmic networks is consistent with mechanical integration between networks. MTs, F-actin, and organelles mechanically interact via many motor and non-motor proteins present in Xenopus egg extracts, and nonspecific steric and hydrodynamic interactions may also contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 and C50 provide a mechanistic interpretation of the co-movement observations. The interpretation (C93) follows logically from the extensive co-movement data. The existence of mechanical interactions (C94) and presence of relevant proteins (C95) are well-supported by multiple literature citations. The speculation about nonspecific interactions (C96) is appropriately qualified as a possibility. This represents a reasonable synthesis of the findings.

results.result: Dynein-mediated inward organelle movement relative to MTs occurs over ~50 µm at the aster periphery. All organelles can move inwards in a dynein-dependent manner and may serve as dynein anchors. The ER may be the predominant dynein anchor because it and mitochondria are most abundant, and the ER moved inwards fastest and to the greatest extent.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C103, C109-C111 synthesize findings about organelle movement and dynein anchoring. The ~50 µm distance (C102) is supported by Figure 7 data. The comparison to other systems (C103) provides useful context. The conclusion that all organelles can serve as dynein anchors (C110) is supported by the movement data for ER, mitochondria, and acidic organelles. The inference that ER is the predominant anchor (C111) is reasonable based on abundance and movement data, though direct evidence for dynein recruitment is limited.

results.result: The molecular mechanism that slows organelle movement inside asters is unknown. F-actin partially accounts for slowing (affecting both organelles and beads), but organelles slow inside asters even when F-actin is fragmented while beads do not. Non-dynein interactions between organelles and MTs may cause a braking effect, with candidate mechanisms including opposing motors, tip tracking factors, brake proteins, or nonspecific interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 present a careful analysis of what is known and unknown about organelle braking. The statement that the mechanism is unknown (C115) is honest. The evidence that F-actin contributes (C116) but doesn't fully explain the effect (C117) is supported by comparing organelle and bead behavior (Figures 7, 8). The hypothesis about non-dynein braking (C118) and list of candidates (C119) are appropriately presented as speculation. The negative result for opposing motors (C120) helps narrow possibilities.

results.result: A model is proposed where at the aster periphery, organelles flow inwards while MTs flow outwards, but in the aster interior, organelles and MTs flow outwards together. Moving asters advect cytosol, generating hydrodynamic forces. The aster is better conceptualized as a deformable gel where the midplane is softer than the interior, with MTOCs moving in response to forces on the gel surface and possibly internal stresses.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127, C129-C130 present an integrated model (Figure 9) synthesizing the major findings. The flows described (C123-C125) are directly supported by the data. The role of convective flow (C126) and F-actin asymmetry (C127) are reasonable inferences. The gel conceptual framework (C129) is well-motivated by the deformation data (C40) and provides a more accurate description than rigid body models. The speculation about force mechanisms (C130) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Re-analysis of zebrafish egg videos suggests that lipid droplets move slowly outwards once embedded in asters, and PIV analysis shows outward flow of MTs at the same speed as lipid droplets, suggesting large asters in zebrafish eggs may also exhibit co-movement of MTs and organelles.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are based on re-analysis of published videos (Wühr et al., 2010, Video 14). While the observations (C106, C107) appear to be accurately described, this is a preliminary analysis of data from another study. The suggestion of co-movement in zebrafish (C108) is appropriately qualified as tentative. More rigorous analysis with multiple markers and quantification would be needed to definitively establish co-movement in zebrafish eggs.

results.result: In fixed Xenopus eggs, the ER was distributed all over the asters with some enrichment near centrosomes and the cortex. The lack of strong ER enrichment at centrosomes called into question the length-dependent pulling model with the ER as a dynein anchor.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C20 are based on immunofluorescence of fixed eggs (Figure 1B',C'). While the observation of ER distribution (C19) is supported by the images, the inference that this calls into question the length-dependent pulling model (C20) is premature. Fixed images provide only a snapshot and cannot reveal dynamics. The subsequent live imaging in extracts (C62-C64) shows that even with intact F-actin, only modest ER enrichment occurs, which better supports this conclusion. The fixed egg data alone are insufficient to challenge the model.

results.result: The identity of the dynein adapter on egg organelles is unknown. Eggs contain abundant lipid droplets and yolk platelets that are removed during extract preparation and could constitute additional dynein anchors.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C113 accurately identify gaps in knowledge. The statement that the dynein adapter identity is unknown (C112) is honest and important. The speculation about lipid droplets and yolk platelets (C113) is reasonable given their abundance in eggs and removal during extract preparation, though this remains untested. These represent appropriate acknowledgments of limitations and future directions.
